children.text: What you wear in Egypt isn't only a packing question.

How you take the heat. How you enter religious sites. Whether you walk markets and old towns without attracting extra eyes. Whether evenings on the Nile and desert mornings don't tire you with cold. Clothing shapes the day's mobility a lot.
The base isn't difficult. Light, loose, modestly covering. That fits the climate and the culture best.

Many travellers think showing skin keeps them cooler in hot countries. In Egypt, not always. Given direct sun, dry air, and reflection off stone and sand, thin linen or cotton long sleeves are often more comfortable than sleeveless. Covering skin isn't only modest; it is practical sun protection.
The base idea
In Egypt, plan to cover shoulders and knees in public.

For women, wide-leg trousers, longer skirts, light long-sleeve shirts, a thin overlayer, and a scarf work well. For men, not-too-short trousers, cotton or linen shirts, and sleeved T-shirts are the base. Body-clinging clothing, see-through fabric, and very short shorts are best avoided outside Red Sea resorts and the inside of hotels.
This isn't about erasing your style. It is about reading the temperature of a place. The same outfit reads differently in
Cairo
's Zamalek or a hotel restaurant than around an Islamic Cairo mosque, in an Upper Egyptian town, or in an oasis like Siwa.
Cairo
Cairo is one city with many social faces.
Along the Nile, in Zamalek, and at New Cairo malls, international-city dressing mixes naturally. In Islamic Cairo,
Khan el-Khalili
, local markets, and old residential streets, more modest dressing walks easier.

For a Cairo day, base on light clothes covering shoulders and knees. If a mosque visit is possible, women should carry a larger scarf to cover hair. Men and women both need legs properly covered in mosques. With shoes off in many places, easy-on, easy-off shoes help.
Some mosques lend cover cloth at the entrance; you don't need to rely on it. Your own scarf or light overlayer is far easier.
At the sites
Pyramids, Karnak, the
Valley of the Kings
, Hatshepsut,
Abu Simbel
. At these, sun protection matters more than religious dress codes.
The sites use the body more than they look. Stone floors are uneven, sand gets into shoes, shade is limited. On
the Giza plateau
and
Luxor
's west bank, the sun beats down and heat reflects off limestone and sand.

Recommended: pale long-sleeve shirts, loose trousers or a longer skirt, a brimmed hat, sunglasses, and walking shoes. Sandals work; closed-toe shoes are safer. Tomb entrances, temple steps, and unpaved paths have more small steps than expected.
Inside Valley of the Kings tombs and pyramid interiors, the air differs from outside. Narrow, hot, sometimes humid. Light, easy-moving clothing suits.
Luxor and
Aswan
In Luxor and Aswan, more situations feel more conservative than Cairo.

Inside temples and hotels, the sight of tourists is familiar; in town souks, on the Corniche, and near residential areas, exposed clothing stands out. Especially for women, choosing longer clothing reduces the load of walking.
Heat response matters. Upper Egyptian summer is very strong, and spring and autumn days get hot too. Avoid dark, thick fabric and choose white, off-white, pale grey, and light blue.

Winter nights cool down. Along the Nile, at desert-side hotels, at sound and light shows, and on early-morning balloon tours, a light overlayer can be needed. Pack only for daytime heat and night surprises you.
Red Sea resorts
In
Hurghada
, Sharm el-Sheikh,
Dahab
, and
Marsa Alam
, the dress sense shifts.
At hotel pools, private beaches, and on dive boats, swimwear or rash guards are fine. The main Red Sea resorts run as international tourist places.
Outside the resort, the story changes. In town restaurants, local shops, public beaches, and markets, carry an overlayer. Walking through town in swimwear alone isn't natural in Egypt.

For diving and snorkelling, rash guards and longer board shorts are very useful. Prevents sunburn, comfortable on board, and culturally less awkward. On the Red Sea, skin-protecting clothing is the practical one.
Desert and oasis
In the Western Desert and Sinai, dress depends on the place even more.
Siwa Oasis

is a conservative land with its own Amazigh culture inside Egypt. Walking the town, long sleeves and long trousers or a long skirt are natural. In Bahariya, Farafra, Dakhla, and Kharga oases, modest dressing fits in local towns too.
In the desert, day and night gap is large. Sun and sand-wind by day, cold by night. A light long sleeve, scarf, hat, and overlayer. The combination matters more than it looks.

In Sinai, the seaside of Sharm and Dahab is relatively free; for St. Catherine's Monastery and inland Bedouin areas, more formal dress is needed. At the monastery, cover shoulders and knees; women should have a scarf for hair.
What helps to bring
The most useful piece of clothing in Egypt is a light large scarf.

Cover hair or shoulders at a mosque. Protect the neck from sun. Layer in strong air-conditioning or restaurants. Block sand in the desert. Use on the Nile at night. A single small cloth absorbs a lot.

Shoes matter too. In Egypt, you rarely walk only on clean paved roads. Sites, cobbles, markets, sand, jetties, steps. Walking, anti-slip, and ideally toe-protected shoes suit. Travelling on beach sandals only isn't recommended.
Fabrics — cotton, linen, light quick-dry. Denim is heavy, slow to dry, and unsuited to hot seasons. Carry fewer easy-wash, easy-combine clothes rather than many.
Common confusions

Women don't need to cover the head all the time. Foreign travellers walking public streets with hair visible is normal. In mosques it becomes necessary. In more conservative areas, covering hair can feel easier for you too.
Shorts work in hotels, resorts, and beaches. Avoid in Cairo markets, Luxor and Aswan towns, and religious sites. Even for men, very short shorts or sleeveless shirts can look careless in some places.
Black is fine but disadvantaged in heat. In Upper Egypt and the desert especially, pale colours are clearly easier.
In sum
Dressing well in Egypt doesn't mean dressing to be invisible.
Fitting the heat. Walking long. Entering religious sites naturally. Not creating extra friction in markets and towns. Receiving the gaps between resort and town, hotel and mosque, day and night.
Cover shoulders, cover knees, carry a light cloth.
That alone makes many places in Egypt much easier to walk.

deck: Cairo mosques, Luxor ruins, Red Sea resorts, desert nights — a clothing guide for being comfortable and natural in Egypt.
